title: Strict slack lets one value be deleted from every neighbourhood
statement: Let a family of finite sets be indexed by a finite set s in which every nonempty subset has strictly fewer elements than its neighbourhood. Then for any value v, s still satisfies Hall's condition against the family with v deleted from every member.

formal.statement: theorem Nat.Hall.hallCondition_sdiff_singleton_of_strict : ((x0 : AxNat.Finset) -> ((x1 : AxNat) -> ((x2 : ((x2 : AxNat) -> AxNat.Finset)) -> ((x3 : ((x3 : AxNat.Finset) -> ((x4 : ((x4 : AxNat) -> ((x5 : Eq.{1} Bool (AxNat.Finset.memB x3 x4) Bool.true) -> Eq.{1} Bool (AxNat.Finset.memB x0 x4) Bool.true))) -> ((x5 : AxNat.lt AxNat.zero (AxNat.Finset.card x3)) -> AxNat.lt (AxNat.Finset.card x3) (AxNat.Finset.card (AxNat.Hall.unionOver x2 x3)))))) -> AxNat.Hall.HallCondition x0 (fun (x4 : AxNat) => AxNat.Finset.sdiff (x2 x4) (AxNat.Finset.singleton x1))))))

notes: THE NON-CRITICAL BRANCH of Hall's inductive step, and the counterpart of F:hall-critical-subset-split. When no proper nonempty subset is critical every nonempty subset has strict slack, and the slack pays for committing one index to one of its neighbours: deleting that single value from every member of the family leaves Hall's condition intact. The strict hypothesis is guarded by `0 < card w` and the guard is NOT cosmetic -- at the empty subset the strict inequality would read `0 < card (unionOver nb empty)`, which is false; that case is discharged by `Nat.zero_le`, DECIDED with `Nat.lt_or_ge` rather than assumed. Hall's condition at s is deliberately not a hypothesis: it would be redundant, since the strict hypothesis is stronger wherever it applies and the conclusion is free where it does not. The successor step is definitional -- `Nat.add` recurses on its right argument, so `add x 1` IS `succ x` by iota. ADR-1644. Hall's marriage theorem itself is NOT established.
